newsitem.title: USA: Election complicates U.S. moves in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Election complicates U.S. moves in Israel.

text.p: Israel caught the United States off guard with the most serious threat yet to Mideast peace, which comes a difficult time -- ahead of elections when Washington's room to manoeuvre is limited by domestic politics.

President Bill Clinton has touted peace between Arabs and Jews as one of his primary foreign policy achievements. But this week's outbreak of fighting between Israel and Palestinians has left his administration scrambling to calm the violence and salvage -- if possible -- the landmark Oslo Accords and the broader peace process they underpin.

It is not the only problem facing Clinton on the foreign policy front. There is new instability in Iraq, continuing serious concerns about Bosnia and growing anxiety about the peace Clinton brought to Haiti with thousands of U.S. troops.

But the Israel-Palestinian conflict may be the most serious, igniting in a flash and exacerbating existing tensions between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government and other Arab states.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has made countless trips to the Middle East, and other senior U.S. officials were on the telephone from Wednesday to Thursday with Israeli, Palestinian and other Arab leaders. They urged Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to restore calm and return to the negotiating table.

But still the fighting continued, resulting in more Palestinan and Israeli deaths and prompting Israel to deploy tanks and helicopters into the West Bank and Gaza -- a show of force not seen since Israel captured the land in 1967.

Clinton finally weighed in personally on Thursday, publicly declaring that "I asked both sides to end this violence, to get back to the business of the peace ... to resolve their differences through negotiations."

He also regretted the "injuries and loss of life" in the West Bank and Gaza in the last two days and said "it points to the urgency of both sides not only to end the violence but to take positive steps to resolve the issues that divide them."
Significantly, Clinton made it a point not to lay blame on Israel for the crisis, although many officials and experts say that is where it belongs.

"Concern is growing about the whole situation and part of that concern is that action (to quell the crisis) is not being taken quickly enough ... I think the onus might be on Israel at this stage," one U.S. official told Reuters.
Clinton, who has staked so much credibility on Mideast peace, has some delicate balancing to do and experts agree domestic politics complicates this.

If he came down too hard on Israel Clinton could alienate -- six weeks before an election -- American Jews who are a potent voting constituency and have embraced him as the most pro-Israel president in history. He could also so anger Israelis and Netanyahu's hardline government that it would provoke a backlash.
But he must continue to be perceived as fair and genuinely protective of Palestinian interests if the United States is to continue to function as a credible broker in the region.
"It's a train wreck," said Arab-American leader James Zogby of the violence that erupted when Netanyahu opened an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy places in Jerusalem.
The incident catalysed Arab anger over Netanyahu's failure to extend Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza and seriously to undertake final status negotiations.

"Clearly this current (Israeli) government has not made strategic decision yet that it wants to support peace. They use the words, talk the talk but ...are not committed to the strategic goals of peace with the Palestinians," Zogby said.

Zogby, who heads an Arab-American group advising the Clinton campaign, said he hoped Clinton would tell Netanyahu Israel could jeopardise economic benefits it has gained from peacemaking and again be isolated diplomatically if he does not follow through on Israel's peace commitments.

Robert Lifton, an American Jew who chairs the Israel Policy Forum, said he does not believe Netanyahu opened the tunnel to deliberately provoke Palestinians but was "unaware" of the anger building among them over unemployment and Israel's failure to move forward on the peace process.

Netanyahu "was removing Palestinians' hope by saying that (Israel) will not discuss statehood and Jerusalem and taking off the table topics that were final status issues" which everyone knew would be difficult and emotional," he said.
"When you leave people with nothing they erupt."

Clinton must make clear that Netanyahu has "to face reality and that is there is an agreement and they committed to pursue that agreement...Their election slogan was peace with security" and does not mean they have a licence to stop the peace process altogether, Lifton said.
